newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai budget cut seen building economic confidence.
newsitem.headline: Thai budget cut seen building economic confidence.

text.p: Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan on Wednesday won cabinet approval for a proposed budget cut, a move designed to help Thailand return to its balanced, deficit-free budget policy after a brief disruption this year.
The move was also expected to build confidence in the economy and help boost the bearish stock market, analysts said.
Amnuay asked the cabinet to trim the 1997/1998 (October/ September) fiscal budget by 26.59 billion baht ($1.02 billion) to offset a sharp decline in tax revenue since mid-1996.

Next year's austerity budget of 982 billion baht represents just a four percent increase from estimated 1996/1997 government spending of 944 billion baht, the smallest year-on-year growth in more than a decade.

Amnuay's action, mostly affecting fixed government spending with little impact on infrastructure projects, was designed to convince a disillusioned market that Thailand would not abandon fiscal and monetary disciplies despite its current economic problems, analysts said.
Amnuay told reporters the 1997/1998 budget cut would not hurt Thai economic growth next year, when the country's gross domestic product is expected to expand at least six percent.
"It is a good gesture that should ease market concern about the economy," Songglod Bhichaikul of United Securities Plc.

Brokers said the budget cut represented much-needed positive news for the bearish Thai stock market. The cut comes on the heels of Amnuay's announcement last weekend that commercial banks would pool a 50 billion baht fund to boost the bourse.
The SET Index advanced for the third straight session on Wednesday, gaining 3.31 percent to close at 596.19 on active 6.3 billion baht turnover.

The rally was long in coming. The index, a broad indicatorof economic confidence, has tumbled about 33 percent since January as growing problems in property and finance sectors and weak exports prompted investors to dump shares.
Prior to its current economic downturn, Thailand enjoyed a hefty government budget surplus in each of the previous nine years.
Amnuay said this week the government would have to shelve its earlier plan to give civil servants a five percent bonus salary during 1997/1998.
A sharp slowdown in Thailand's economy has forced the government to miss its tax revenue target by a wide margin this year.
Its original 984 billion baht tax revenue target for the 1996/1997 year has been trimmed twice, to 925 billion in January and to 880.8 billion this week.
The revenue shortfall this year would leave the government with its first budget deficit in 10 years of about 63.2 billion baht, according to the Budget Bureau.

To help narrow the budget deficit this year and boost tax collection in 1998, the cabinet on Wednesday decided to raise or introduce nine excise taxes, mostly on luxury imported products. The move was expected to earn the government about 7.7 billion baht annually.
The economy is expected to expand five to six percent this year against 6.7 percent in 1996 and 8.7 percent the previous year.
